column2: Start at height one. Here are two drawing rules. On the left, climb at a constant rate of one. On the right, let the rate equal the current height. At the beginning they agree. But will they keep drawing the same curve?

Take one small step to the right. Both rules begin with slope one, so their first straight steps agree. Now read the height again. The left rule still says slope one. The right rule asks for a steeper slope, because its height has increased.

Repeat the procedure. Read the height, use it as the slope, and take another short step. The left drawing is a straight line. The right drawing keeps steepening. Its straight steps are approximations. During a step the true height would already have changed, so the true slope would change too.

Use shorter steps and read the height more often. We keep the same axes and the same starting height. The old approximation stays in grey. The new one climbs slightly higher. Shortening the steps again brings the new drawings closer together. Agreement in a picture is evidence to investigate, not a proof of a limit.

A curve whose slope equals its height would solve our drawing rule exactly. We have not yet proved that the stepped approximations reach such a curve, or that only one such curve starts at height one. To answer those questions, we will build an exact function, term by term. That is where the factorials will come from.

Our drawing rule asks for a function whose derivative equals itself, starting at one. Try a polynomial. Put its coefficients in boxes, one box for each power. Differentiation moves each term one column left and multiplies its coefficient by the power it came from. To make the two rows agree, what must the coefficient of x be?

It must be one. Now the derivative of b times x squared is two b times x. That must match the x term above, whose coefficient is one. So b is one half. The derivative of c times x cubed is three c times x squared. To match one half, c must be one sixth.

Continue the same rule. Each coefficient is the previous one divided by the next whole number. We get one, one, one half, one sixth, one twenty-fourth. Those denominators are factorials. As we add terms, watch the polynomial change on the same axes. These curves are partial sums, not yet the exact solution.

A finite polynomial cannot finish the job. Differentiation removes its highest power. With infinitely many terms, another term can supply each missing power. But dots are not a proof. We need to know that the sum exists and that differentiating it term by term is legitimate.

Choose any bounded interval, from minus R to R. The ratio of one absolute term to the previous one is at most R divided by its index. Eventually that ratio is at most one half. So the remaining terms fit beneath a shrinking geometric tail. The same argument works for the derivative series. Both converge uniformly on each bounded interval, which justifies differentiating term by term.

Call the sum E of x. The shifted coefficient rows now match all the way across: E prime equals E, and E of zero is one. We built a solution to our drawing rule. We still owe three explanations: why adding inputs multiplies outputs, why the stepped approximations reach this curve, and why it is the only solution with that starting value. The series gives us a way to answer all three.

We built E from its power series. Why should adding inputs multiply outputs? Put the terms of E of x across the top, and the terms of E of y down the side. Each square contains one product. The complete grid goes on forever. We are showing its first corner, not pretending that sixteen products are the whole answer.

Instead of collecting the products by rows, collect them by total degree. Degree zero has just one square, containing one. Degree one has two squares: x and y. Their sum is x plus y. Now inspect the three squares of degree two. Before we combine them, can you recognize their sum?

They give x squared over two, plus x y, plus y squared over two. Factor out one half. Inside the brackets is x squared plus two x y plus y squared: the square of x plus y. So this diagonal contributes the square of the sum x plus y, divided by two. The factorial in the denominator has survived.

The degree-three diagonal works the same way. In general, multiplying a degree-m diagonal by m factorial gives the binomial coefficients. The binomial theorem combines that diagonal into the sum x plus y, raised to the m, divided by m factorial. We have shown the complete diagonals through degree three here. Higher ones continue beyond the visible corner.

There is one analytic permission slip. Both series converge absolutely, so their product can be regrouped by diagonals without changing its sum. The diagonals are precisely the terms of E at the sum, x plus y. Therefore E of x times E of y equals E of the sum, x plus y. The multiplication law came from the factorials and convergence, not from naming the function exponential.

Set y equal to minus x. The product is E of zero, which is one, so E never vanishes. For a real x, apply the same law to two copies of half x. E of x is the square of a nonzero real number, so it is positive. Since its derivative is itself, it is increasing. Those familiar properties now follow from what we built.

Now we can name a number. Call E of one by the small letter e. The law says E of two is e times e, and E of three is e cubed. Roots give fractions, reciprocals give negatives, and continuity fills in the rest. That is when writing E of x as e to the x becomes a result, not a label.

Return to the short straight steps. Each step took the current height and climbed by that height times the step's width. But climbing by a fraction of your own height is the same as multiplying your height. So a step one quarter wide multiplies by five quarters, whatever the height was. Four steps make five quarters to the fourth power, the endpoint we already drew.

Give one unit of time this fixed width, and split it into n cells. Now let the slope be x times the current height. Over that one unit of time, the fractional rate x gives each of n steps the multiplier one plus x over n. After all the steps, we have that multiplier raised to the n-th power. For a rate of one, this is the familiar compound-growth construction of e. More cells keep raising its endpoint, by less and less.

Now put those endpoints on the graph of our series. Change the rate, and the endpoint lands near the curve at that input, for rates above zero and below it. Near is still not a proof. Why should that limit be our series? Expand the finite product.

Each cell offers two choices. Keep its one, or take its x over n. Multiplying out the product means making those choices in every possible way. With four cells, that is sixteen ways, and they sort themselves by how many cells took x. For x squared, two cells must take it, and six pairs of cells can do that. So the coefficient of x squared is six times a quarter times a quarter, six sixteenths.

For any n and any k, count the same way. Pick cells one at a time. There are n options, then n minus one, then n minus two, until k cells are picked. Every set of k cells was counted k factorial times, so divide by k factorial. There is our factorial, earned a second way.

Now each picked cell brings its one over n, and those share out across the picks. So the coefficient of x to the k is one over k factorial, multiplied by a short chain of correction factors. The chain runs one, one minus one over n, one minus two over n, and so on. For our six sixteenths, that is one half, times one, times three quarters. Ask for more cells than exist, and one factor is exactly zero.

Hold k still, and let n grow. Here each bar shows how much of the series coefficient the product has reached. For any fixed k, every correction factor approaches one as n grows. The coefficient approaches exactly the coefficient in our series. The columns fill one at a time, but at every n, far columns are still nearly empty. If every column fills eventually, must the whole sum arrive?

Matching each fixed coefficient is not enough by itself, because there are also more and more terms. Here is a sum where that reasoning fails. Take n terms, each equal to one over n. Every fixed term shrinks to zero, so column by column the limit looks like zero. Yet the total is one, for every n. The weight slips out to columns further and further away.

Here is what makes our argument safe. Until k passes n, each correction factor lies between zero and one, and after that the chain is zero, so a whole chain never leaves that range. In absolute value, each finite-product term is no larger than the corresponding exponential-series term. These are the same ceilings we measured for the series, and n does not move them. Our warning sum has no such ceilings. Its column k can reach one over k, and those add up without limit.

Now measure the distance to E of x. It is at most the total of the gaps between each bar and its ceiling. Say we want that distance below one hundredth. Choose a cut before choosing n. Beyond the cut, every gap fits under the series tail, for every n at once.

We already know that series has a small tail, so push the cut out until the tail is small enough. Before the cut sit only finitely many columns, and each of their gaps closes. First make the shared tail small, then make the finitely many remaining coefficients close. That proves the whole expression converges.

Nothing in that argument asked x to be positive. We redraw with only sixteen cells, just so the gaps under the ceilings are wide enough to see. Now slide to minus three halves. The odd terms turn negative, so the bars alternate up and down. In absolute value they are the same bars under the same ceilings. The bound on the card still uses one thousand twenty-four cells and the same cut, and it holds here too.

Push further, to minus three. One cell gives minus two. Two cells give one quarter, and three give exactly zero. Four cells give almost nothing, and then the values climb toward E of minus three. Decay needs a positive multiplier in every step, so the decay reading needs more than three cells. The algebra never asked for that. It never asked the values to climb steadily, and it never used a logarithm.

So for every real x, that n-th power approaches E of x. For bigger inputs, this argument asks for a later cut and more cells, but every input arrives. A rate of one gives the number e, one special case of this limit. A rate of x for one unit of time and a rate of one for x units of time make the same product. So the stepped drawing out to any input reaches the curve at that input. That pays the second debt.

We constructed a function whose derivative equals itself. Could a different function obey the same rule and start at the same height? What we just proved does not settle that. The steps reach E, but nothing yet forces every solution to follow our steps.

So build a test. Take any function y that has a derivative, and multiply it by E of minus x. Differentiate that product. One contribution is y prime times E of minus x. The other comes from E of minus x itself, whose slope is minus E of minus x, by the chain rule. Together they make the difference y prime minus y, multiplied by E of minus x.

Try it on functions that break the rule. Our degree-two polynomial starts at height one, but its derivative loses its top term. Its product with E of minus x tilts. On these axes, degree four breaks the rule less, and tilts less. E of minus x is never zero, so the product can only be level where y prime equals y. Suppose a function obeys the rule everywhere. What must its product do?

It stays level. One contribution is the proposed function times E of minus x, and the other is its negative. They cancel. A slope of zero across an interval means a constant value, and at zero that value is one. So y of x times E of minus x equals one, everywhere on that interval.

Now multiply both sides by E of x. The product grid already gave us E of x times E of minus x equals one, so the left side collapses to y of x. The proposed solution must equal E of x everywhere on its interval. That is the rule in both directions. E obeys it, and whatever obeys it is E.

Is this a circle? Follow the arrows. The series gave us E prime equals E, by differentiating term by term. Multiplying series in the grid gave us E of x times E of minus x equals one. Neither step used this result. All we added was the product rule, the chain rule, and the fact that zero slope on an interval means constant. No uniqueness theorem and no logarithm came in. Every arrow points one way.

The word interval is doing work. Cut a gap in the domain, and the far piece can be three times E. Its slope equals its height, and the start at zero never hears about it. So the proposed function needs one unbroken interval containing the starting input, with a derivative at every point.

The same test handles any constant rate k. If y prime equals k times y, multiply by E of minus k t. The contributions cancel again, so y of t equals y of zero times E of k t. For a positive starting amount, positive k gives growth, negative k gives decay, and zero k keeps it constant, while a zero start stays at zero. The rate k has units of one over time, so k t is a pure number, ready to be an input. Whether a real quantity obeys this law is a question for each application.

The power series, the small-multiplier limit and the rate law are three descriptions of the same object. Its powers, derivatives and growth rule fit together because they express the same structure from different sides. All three debts are paid.

We have earned the rule that adding inputs multiplies outputs. Now let us turn that rule into a machine you can hold. Imagine asking the exponential a question backwards. What input produces two? What input produces three? Those input distances will become the markings on our ruler.

Watch the horizontal distance that produces each height. Transfer that distance to a straight rail, and write the height beside it. One belongs at the beginning, because the exponential of zero is one. The gaps shrink as the labels grow. Equal distances do not add equal numbers here. They multiply by equal factors.

We can choose the ruler's unit of length. Let the distance from one to ten be one complete scale. The position of a number is then its base ten logarithm. That name matters less than its job, which is to tell us how far to go to obtain the number. The multiplication law says that the distance for two, followed by the distance for three, is the distance for six.

Copy the scale onto a strip that can slide. Each end mark of a scale is called an index. Move the upper one, the left index, until it sits above the lower two. Every upper marking moves by the same distance. In particular, the upper three now sits above the lower six. We added two distances with our hands, and the labels did the multiplication. The answer came from the spacing, not from an electronic circuit or a hidden table of products.
Try a new calculation before we move anything. If the upper one goes above two and a half, where will the upper four land? Follow the two distances, and make a prediction.

It lands on ten, exactly at the end of this scale. Two and a half times four is ten. But a physical ruler has ends. For four times three, aligning the upper one with the lower four would put the upper three beyond the lower scale. There is no twelve marking out there to read. We need to use the other index.

Bring the upper ten above the lower four instead. Moving from the left index to the right index changes the alignment by one whole scale length. That length represents a factor of ten. The upper three now sits above one point two on the lower scale. Our answer is twelve, because this alignment divided the reading by ten. The scale supplies the significant digits. We must keep track of the decimal place.

This is not a trick confined to the number twelve. Equal ratios occupy equal distances anywhere on the scale. The distance from one to two equals the distance from two to four. So an extra scale length always means another factor of ten. A quick estimate of the answer's size keeps one point two, twelve and one hundred twenty from being confused.

Division reverses the same geometry. Put the upper three above the lower six. Under the upper one, read two. The distance for six minus the distance for three is the distance for two. Nothing about the ruler changed. We simply asked which multiplier would carry three to six.

There is a price for making arithmetic physical. Marks have width, and your eye cannot distinguish arbitrarily close positions. A slide rule gives approximate significant digits, not an unlimited string of exact digits. Its great advantage was replacing lengthy written multiplication and division with alignments and a size estimate. The exponential supplied the multiplication law, and the logarithm turned that law into distances. Next, we will see why the same exponential appears in a laboratory, even when nobody is using a ruler.

A curve can look exponential without having an exponential cause. So before putting our function into a laboratory, ask what the process actually does. Does it remove the same amount each second, or the same fraction of whatever remains? Those are different instructions. We will draw both on the same axes, starting from the same amount.

First, remove a fixed amount per second. The amount falls along a straight line. Now change the instruction: make the removal rate proportional to the amount currently present. A large amount loses material quickly. A smaller amount loses it more slowly. The slope changes because the quantity controlling the slope is changing.

Call the concentration A, and write its rate of change as minus k times A. The minus sign means removal; k is positive and stays constant in this model. This is the rate law we already solved. The concentration is its starting value times e to the minus k t. Chemistry calls this a first-order rate law. Whether a particular reaction follows it must be established from the reaction and its conditions.

Here is a consequence we can see without solving the equation again. Suppose one fixed interval reduces our model amount from one hundred to fifty. Start a second sample at fifty, under the same conditions. Its removal rate is half as large at every corresponding point. Where should it finish after that same interval? Pause before we draw its endpoint.

It finishes at twenty-five. The whole second trajectory is a half-sized copy of the first. The same interval takes fifty to twenty-five, then twenty-five to twelve and a half. We have not subtracted fifty each time. We have multiplied by one half. That repeating interval is the half-life of this model, as long as k stays constant.

The multiplication rule explains why the clock does not care when we restart it. The fraction remaining after one interval and then another is the product of the two fractions. The first interval changes the amount, but it does not change the rule. On the graph, lift out a later segment and rescale its starting height to one. It lies exactly on the original curve.

That conclusion has assumptions. Change the temperature so the rate constant changes, and the same half-life need not persist. Change the rate law so removal depends on the square of the concentration, and the rescaled curves no longer share one clock. Exponentials are useful because a precise rule forces their shape, not because every decreasing curve is secretly exponential.

Our smooth concentration is a macroscopic model. A small collection of individual reacting molecules would not disappear in perfectly synchronized batches. The picture's bar represents an amount, not a promise about which molecule changes next. Keep that distinction as we move to a different application, where the quantity grows toward a ceiling instead of decaying toward zero.

Connect a capacitor to a battery through a resistor. A capacitor stores separated electric charge; the voltage across it grows as that charge builds up. The resistor limits the current. Why does the capacitor charge quickly at first, then creep toward the battery voltage? The battery is not getting tired. The voltage difference that drives the current is shrinking.

Draw the battery voltage as a fixed horizontal level. Below it is the capacitor voltage, which starts at zero. Highlight the vertical gap between them. Ohm's law says the current is that gap divided by the resistance. The capacitor relation says current equals capacitance times the rate at which its voltage changes. Put those two statements together: the voltage rises at a rate proportional to the remaining gap.

The capacitor voltage itself does not satisfy our simple decay equation. But the gap does. When the voltage rises by a small amount, the gap falls by the same amount. Its derivative is minus the gap divided by resistance times capacitance. We have found the exponential by changing what we measure. The gap decays exponentially; the voltage is the battery level minus that decaying gap.

Let us choose an ideal example with a twelve-volt battery, ten thousand ohms of resistance, and one hundred microfarads of capacitance. These are chosen model values, not measurements of a particular device. Resistance times capacitance is one second. This product sets the clock: after one such time interval, the remaining gap is one over e times its starting size.

So after one second, about thirty-six point eight percent of the original gap remains, and about sixty-three point two percent has been filled. The voltage is about seven point five nine volts. Watch three linked readouts: the voltage rises, the gap shrinks, and the current shrinks with the gap. The same moving point determines all three. Their curves are not independent illustrations.

Now keep the battery and capacitor fixed, but double the resistance. Before the second trace moves, predict two things. Does the starting current increase or decrease? And does reaching the same fraction of the battery voltage take more time or less?

The starting current halves, and reaching the same fraction takes twice as long. The resistance appears in the current's denominator and in the time constant. Rescale the time axis of the slower trace by the right factor, and the two voltage curves coincide. We changed the clock, not the shape. Increasing the capacitance has the same effect on the time constant, but it does not halve the initial current when the resistance stays fixed.

This is an ideal circuit model: a constant battery voltage, a linear resistor, a fixed capacitance, and no extra leakage or other components. It approaches the battery voltage without reaching it at a finite time. A real instrument eventually cannot distinguish the remaining gap. That is practical settling, not the exponential suddenly becoming zero. The useful question is how small the gap must be for the job at hand.

In the decay model and the capacitor model, the rate constant really was constant. That assumption did a lot of work. So change it. Picture algae in a pond through a spell of cooling weather. At first each bit of algae makes more. As the water cools, that rate falls, passes through zero, and becomes dying back. Let the rate at each moment depend on the time on the clock, and keep the rest of the rule. The amount still changes in proportion to itself, but that proportion now moves. We invent the numbers for this pond. The rate starts at one, and falls in a straight line through zero at time one, to minus one at time two.

Go back to our tiny multipliers. Cut time into cells. In each cell the rate is nearly steady, so the amount is multiplied by about one plus the rate times the cell's width. A positive rate gives a multiplier above one. A rate of zero gives exactly one. A negative rate gives a multiplier below one. The final amount is the product of all of them. Four cells finish near one point four. But these cells are crude. The rate spends one unit of time above zero and one unit of time below it, at matching sizes. So make a prediction. As the cells shrink, does the amount finish above its start, below its start, or exactly where it began?

Exactly where it began. Here is why. Over one cell, the multiplier is very nearly E applied to the product of the rate and the width. Our multiplication law turns a product of exponentials into the exponential of a sum. That sum is the area under the rate curve, counted negative below the axis. So the amount at any time is E of the area so far. At time two the area above the axis and the area below it cancel, and E of zero is one.

That argument used approximate cells. The exact proof is a test we already own. Call the area so far capital R, so R prime is the rate. Multiply the amount by E of minus R, and differentiate. The two contributions cancel, exactly as they did for a constant rate. So that product never changes, and y equals its start times E of R. The rate only has to be continuous, so that the area has the rate as its slope. It need not be positive, and it need not be constant.

Run the cells again, and the picture agrees. Four cells finish near one point four. Every cell read its rate at its left edge, where this falling rate is highest. Sixteen finish near one point zero nine. One thousand twenty-four finish within about a tenth of a percent of one. Now look at the curve itself. It rises, stops and falls, so it is not an exponential curve. Yet every point on it is E of something. Our function has not changed. Only its input has, and that input runs like a clock that slows, stops and turns back. A clock like that has no single half-life to quote.

Money is where most people meet this formula, so let us be careful about what it says. Take a starting hundred and a quoted rate of twelve percent a year. Credit it once a year, and the hundred becomes one hundred twelve. Credit it monthly, at one percent a month, and it becomes about one hundred twelve dollars and sixty-eight cents. Credit it daily, and it reaches about one hundred twelve dollars and seventy-five cents. Those are our tiny multipliers again, and more cells keep raising the result by less and less. The limit is E of zero point one two, times one hundred, and it is also about one hundred twelve dollars and seventy-five cents.

A yearly percentage change is a way of describing that year's multiplier. A year that multiplies by one point two is a twenty percent gain. A year that multiplies by zero point nine is a ten percent loss. The percentages suggest ten percent overall. The money says one point two times zero point nine, which is one point zero eight, an eight percent gain. Ask which input of E gives one point two. It is about zero point one eight two. That input is the year's continuous rate. For zero point nine it is about minus zero point one zero five. Continuous rates are the ones that add, because adding inputs multiplies outputs. Either order gives the same one hundred eight. Multiplication does not care about order. Now change one thing. At the end of the first year, take out fifty. Does the order of the two years still not matter?

It matters a great deal. Good year first, one hundred becomes one hundred twenty, the fifty comes out, leaving seventy, and the bad year leaves sixty-three. Bad year first, the hundred becomes ninety, the fifty comes out, leaving forty, and the good year leaves forty-eight. Same two multipliers, and a difference of fifteen. Each dollar is multiplied only by the years it stays for. The fifty that left would have become forty-five in one order and sixty in the other. In the rate law this is one more term, the money moving in or out. Each payment starts its own exponential from its own moment, and the total is their sum.

So far, every multiplier was known in advance. Now let chance choose them. Toss a fair coin. Heads multiplies the amount by one point five, and tails multiplies it by zero point six. These are invented numbers, chosen to separate two ideas. They describe no market and no investment. The average of the two multipliers is one point zero five, a gain of five percent per toss. Now toss a hundred times. Does a typical run grow by about five percent per toss?

A typical run shrinks. Because multipliers compound, the ruler is the right picture, with distances measured as inputs of E. Heads moves us right by the distance for one point five. Tails moves us left by the distance for zero point six, and that distance is longer. A head and a tail together multiply by zero point nine. A run with exactly fifty of each ends at zero point nine to the fiftieth power, about half a percent of where it began. That is the middle run. Five heads more or fewer changes the result by a factor of about a hundred. So runs scatter widely, but the middle of them sits far below the start. Only about fourteen runs in a hundred finish above the start. The average over all runs really is about one hundred thirty-one and a half times the start. But under three runs in a hundred, those with sixty heads or more, supply over ninety-nine percent of that average. An average across many parallel runs is not what a single run experiences.

One assumption is still hiding. The proportion was the same however large the amount became. Must growth continue exponentially forever? In a population, or a product spreading through a market, the proportional rate can depend on how much room is left. A simple model multiplies the rate by one minus the amount divided by a capacity. Here are both rules with the same start, eight percent of capacity, and the same rate. How long before you could tell them apart from the curves alone?

Not for a while. After half a unit of time, they differ by only about five percent. After one unit, about fourteen percent. Then the capacity bends one curve flat while the other runs off the top of the chart. An early stretch of noisy data can hardly tell you which curve you are on. Just as with the capacitor, changing what we measure turns this into something we already know. Measure one over the amount, and its distance from one over the capacity decays exactly exponentially. The caution about early data applies to an economy's growth rate too. It is measured after the fact, and the conditions behind it can change.

So each assumption buys one piece of the formula, and each failure has its own replacement. A constant rate gives E evaluated at k times t. A rate that changes with the clock gives E of the area under it. Money moving in or out gives one exponential per payment. Chance in the multipliers splits the question. For the average over many runs, average the multipliers. For a typical run, average the distances on the ruler. Feedback from the amount itself needs a different equation. These are ways of doing the arithmetic. They are not forecasts, and none of this is advice about what to do with money.

Every rate so far has been a real number. A positive rate grows, and a negative rate decays. Take a weight on a spring, with units chosen so that its acceleration is minus its position. Apply a rate twice and you get the rate squared, and no real rate has a negative square. So add one new number, i, whose square is minus one, and keep every other rule. Now look at what our machinery really asked for. It added and multiplied, in either order. It divided by whole numbers. And it measured sizes, because regrouping the grid needed the sizes of the terms to have a finite sum. Complex numbers can do all of that. Picture one as an arrow from zero to a point in the plane. Go x steps across and y steps up, and the point is x plus i y. Multiply by i, and every arrow does the same simple thing. It turns a quarter turn counterclockwise. One becomes i, and i becomes minus one. Take one and a half across and one up. Multiply by i, and it becomes minus one plus one and a half i. In general, x plus i y becomes minus y plus i x.

Feed our series an imaginary input, i times t. Each term is exactly as large as the term for t alone, so the same ceilings bound it, and the sum exists for every t. Differentiating term by term brings a factor of i out front. So the point z, equal to E evaluated at i times t, obeys a rate law with a rate of i. Now compare three rates. A rate of one pushes a point straight out along its own arrow. A rate of minus one pulls it straight in. A rate of i takes that arrow, turns it a quarter turn, and uses the result as the velocity. Where will the output travel?

The velocity is always at a right angle to the arrow. A push sideways can only move the point along, never out and never in. Check it in coordinates. Write z as x plus i y. The law says x prime is minus y, and y prime is x. The slope of x squared plus y squared is two x times minus y, plus two y times x, and those cancel. So the distance from zero never changes. Start at one, and it stays one. The speed is the length of i times z, and that is also one.

A point at distance one, moving at speed one, always counterclockwise. That is a walk around the unit circle. After time t it has walked a distance t along the circle. Distance along the unit circle is exactly what an angle in radians measures, so the point sits at angle t. And the coordinates of the point at angle t are the cosine and the sine. So E evaluated at i times t equals cosine t plus i sine t. Nobody assumed this. The left side came from our series, the right side came from a circle, and the rate law forced them to be the same point. It is called Euler's formula.

Now follow the two coordinates separately. The horizontal shadow traces cosine, and the vertical shadow traces sine. Each one feeds the other. The slope of cosine is minus sine, and the slope of sine is cosine. Those are the same two equations, x prime is minus y and y prime is x. Apply the rate twice, and you get i times i, which is minus one. So the acceleration is minus the position. That is the weight on the spring we began with, and it is why a spring swings in the same two waves.

We built our function in three ways, and the circle should show up in each of them. Start with tiny multipliers. To reach time pi, split the time into n cells. Each step takes the current arrow, turns a copy a quarter turn, shrinks that copy to pi over n of its length, and adds it on. With four cells the steps are big, and we clearly leave the circle. Every step runs at a right angle to its own arrow, so every step ends farther from zero than it began. The walk around the circle says one place. As the cells get smaller, do these paths agree?

They agree, and they land on minus one. Each step multiplies the length by a number just above one, the square root of one plus the square of pi over n. That excess has size one over n squared, so all n of them together are only of size one over n. Meanwhile the turning angles add up closer and closer to pi. Sixteen cells land here, sixty-four land closer, and one thousand twenty-four land within half a percent of minus one. The limit proof needs nothing new, because it only ever compared the sizes of terms.

Now the series. Use the imaginary unit times pi as the input, and draw each term as an arrow, tip to tail. Each new term is the previous one, turned a quarter turn and multiplied by pi over k. While k is less than pi, that factor is bigger than one, so the arrows grow and the path swings far from zero. Once k passes pi, the factorial takes over, the arrows shrink, and the path spirals in. It spirals to the same place, minus one.

Three pictures, one landing point. The walk, the polygons and the spiral all say that E of i pi is minus one. We usually write this value as e to the i pi. That notation is not repeated multiplication, and nobody multiplies e by itself i pi times. It names our function at that input, and it has earned the name because the multiplication law still holds. So here is the famous line. E to the i pi, plus one, equals zero. It is called Euler's identity. The pi is there because half of the unit circle has length pi. The minus one is there because a half turn reverses every arrow.

Our multiplication law has a new meaning on the circle. E evaluated at i times s, times E evaluated at i times t, equals E evaluated at i times the sum. Multiplying these arrows adds their angles, so the circle is a slide rule for turns. Write both sides in cosines and sines, and the two angle-addition formulas appear at once. Split our series into even and odd powers of t, and there are the cosine and sine series too.

Now let the rate have both parts, a real part called a, plus i times a real coefficient called w. The multiplication law splits the result into E evaluated at a times t, times E evaluated at i times w times t. The real part sets the length, and the imaginary part sets the angle. A negative real part spirals inward. One law now contains decay, growth, rotation and the spirals between them.

Step back and count what we built. A series of factorials. A product of tiny multipliers. A rate law with exactly one solution. A rule that adding inputs multiplies outputs, once its slope at zero is one. A ruler that multiplies by sliding. Five descriptions, and they turned out to be one object.

Each description also runs backward, and the backward machine is the natural logarithm. Measure the ruler in the exponential's own unit, and a number's position is its natural logarithm. Our slide rule used the same marks with a longer unit. Ask the rate law how long growth must run from one to reach x, and the answer changes at rate one over x. Ask the tiny multipliers which rate gives x after n cells. Take the n-th root of x, subtract one, and multiply by n. Ask the series, and a new series appears, with alternating signs and no factorials, and it only reaches so far.

So far, each question had one answer. On the real number line there is no difficulty, because every positive number has exactly one input. On a circle, E of zero and E evaluated at two pi times i are the same point. The same output can come from more than one input. The logarithm has more to reveal, and that is where our companion video goes next.
